title: Finite unramified isomorphism schemes for stable curves
statement: Let $k$ be a field and let $g\geq2$. The stack $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,0}$ of stable unpointed genus-$g$ curves, as defined in [def-sfb-stable-pointed-moduli-groupoids], is of finite type over $k$ and has finite unramified diagonal. Explicitly, for every $k$-scheme $T$ and two stable unpointed genus-$g$ families $C\to T$ and $D\to T$, the functor on $T$-schemes $T'$ sending $T'$ to the set of $T'$-isomorphisms $C_{T'}\xrightarrow{\sim}D_{T'}$ is represented by a finite unramified $T$-scheme. Unramified means locally of finite type with diagonal an open immersion. The finite diagonal assertion refers to the 2-fibre-product convention of that definition; in particular the inertia morphism, whose fibre at a curve is its automorphism group scheme, is finite. Fields, schemes, finite type and finite morphisms use [def-weil-field], [def-pc-scheme], [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] and [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism].

proof.text: Put $r=19(g-1)$ and $P(m)=20(g-1)m+1-g$. The ten-canonical parameter theorem gives a projective finite-type Hilbert scheme $Z$ and a locally closed subscheme $J$ parametrizing projectively framed stable curves. Write $J$ as a closed subscheme of an open $V\subseteq Z$. A field is Noetherian (its only ideals are zero and the whole field), so the finite-type-over-Noetherian theorem makes $Z$ Noetherian. The open-subscheme theorem makes every open of $Z$ quasi-compact; in particular $V\to Z$ is a quasi-compact open immersion, and hence of finite type by the cited open-immersion theorem. The closed immersion $J\to V$ is of finite type directly from the definition: on an affine open its inverse image is $\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)$, a cyclic $A$-module and a finitely generated $A$-algebra. Composition gives $J\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ of finite type. This uses the parameter theorem's locally closed locus only, not any claim that the whole stable stack is already of finite type.

source.place: Tag 0E9B (lemma-stable-quasi-compact), bounded pluricanonical parameter argument; reuse the existing ten-canonical parameter node instead of introducing a second tricanonical parameter.

proof.text: Write $\mathcal M=\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,0}$. The existing unpointed-coarse theorem states, in particular, that this very groupoid is an algebraic stack smooth over $k$. Thus a smooth scheme atlas has smooth composite to $\operatorname{Spec}k$. Such a composite is locally finitely presented by the smooth-morphism definition, hence locally of finite type (a finitely presented algebra has finitely many generators). This is the atlas definition of local finite type for the stack. For quasi-compactness, let $B$ be any affine $k$-scheme. The scheme $J_B$ is of finite type over $B$ by finite-type base change, so is quasi-compact. Every geometric stable curve over $B$ admits a projective frame of its ten-canonical sections, so $J_B\to\mathcal M_B$ is surjective on geometric isomorphism classes by the parameter theorem. Pulling back any open cover of $|\mathcal M_B|$ gives an open cover of $J_B$; a finite subcover covers $|\mathcal M_B|$ by this surjectivity. Hence $\mathcal M\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is quasi-compact. Together with local finite type this proves finite type. Here finite type for a stack means locally of finite type, checked on smooth atlases, and quasi-compact. No inference from finite type of the coarse scheme alone is made.

source.place: Tags 0E9B and 0E9C (lemma-stable-quasi-compact, theorem-stable-smooth-proper); stacks-morphisms.tex definition-locally-finite-type, finite type = locally finite type and quasi-compact.

proof.text: Set $S=J\times_kJ$. It is a finite-type $k$-scheme: its first projection is a base change of $J\to\operatorname{Spec}k$, and compose with the other structure morphism. Pull back the universal framed curve from each factor to obtain $C_S,D_S$. The parameter theorem supplies their closed ten-canonical embeddings into $\mathbf P^{r-1}_S$, so these are projective in the fixed-projective-space convention required by the existing pointed-Isom theorem. They are flat finitely presented stable genus-$g$ families by what $J$ represents. Apply that theorem with zero marked sections. Its hypothesis is precisely finite type of $S$ over the field, not normality: normality belongs only to its separate generic-extension conclusion. We obtain a finite unramified $S$-scheme $I_S$ representing every unpointed isomorphism between $C_S$ and $D_S$, naturally on all $S$-schemes. We retain these curve automorphisms; a choice of frame in this step parametrizes the curves, and imposes no frame-preservation condition on their isomorphisms.

source.place: Tags 0E7A and 0E9A: finite unramified Isom; use the already split stronger pointed-Isom result, with empty markings, on the finite-type universal-pair base.

proof.text: Now let $T$ be an arbitrary $k$-scheme and $C,D$ the two families in the question. By the parameter theorem, their ten-canonical pushforwards are finite-rank locally free, commute with base change, and have Zariski locally trivial projective-frame torsors. Choose a common Zariski open cover $T=\bigcup_aT_a$ on which both have frames. Each framed family then gives a map $T_a\to J$, and the pair gives $v_a:T_a\to S$. Their underlying curves are the pullbacks of $C_S,D_S$. Form $I_a=T_a\times_{S,v_a}I_S$. Associativity of scheme fibre products identifies its points over any $U\to T_a$ with precisely $\operatorname{Isom}_U(C_U,D_U)$; in particular it parametrizes all isomorphisms, not just those preserving the chosen frames. The finite-morphism base-change statement and the unramified base-change statement show $I_a\to T_a$ is finite unramified. Neither statement requires $T_a$ to be Noetherian or of finite type.

source.place: Tags 0E7A and 0E9A, extension from a framed universal pair by arbitrary base change; morphisms.tex Tags 01WJ and 02GA for the cited scheme base-change tools.

proof.text: On $T_{ab}=T_a\cap T_b$, both $I_a\times_TT_{ab}$ and $I_b\times_TT_{ab}$ represent the same isomorphism functor. Identify them by the unique map sending a curve isomorphism to that same curve isomorphism. In particular the identification for $a=b$ is the identity, reverse identifications are inverses, and on $T_a\cap T_b\cap T_c$ their composites agree because both send every isomorphism to itself. The domain $U_{ab}=I_a\times_TT_{ab}$ is open in $I_a$; the overlap identifications take $U_{ab}\cap U_{ac}$ to $U_{ba}\cap U_{bc}$ since both are the inverse image of the same triple intersection. These are exactly the hypotheses of the scheme-gluing node. It gives a scheme $I$ covered by the $I_a$, with precisely these overlaps. The maps $I_a\to T_a\to T$ agree on them, so the morphism-gluing node gives $I\to T$. The inverse image of $T_a$ is $I_a$: on every chart $I_b$ it is the specified overlap $I_b\times_TT_a$, identified with the corresponding open of $I_a$.

source.place: Tags 01JB and 01JC (lemma-glue, lemma-glue-schemes); canonical-overlap construction and gluing maps.

proof.text: For any $U\to T$, put $U_a=U\times_TT_a$. A morphism $U\to I$ over $T$ is the same as maps $U_a\to I_a$ agreeing on overlaps, by morphism gluing. These maps are the local curve isomorphisms $C_{U_a}\xrightarrow{\sim}D_{U_a}$. Compatible local isomorphisms glue to an isomorphism $C_U\xrightarrow{\sim}D_U$: apply the same morphism-gluing theorem on the inverse images of the $U_a$ in $C_U$, and also to the inverse maps on $D_U$; the two composites are identities because this holds on the cover. The construction is unique and commutes with further pullback since every local representing bijection does. Thus $I$ represents exactly the functor in the question on all $T$-schemes.

source.place: Tag 01JA (section-glueing-schemes), mapping property; the cited general morphism-gluing statement supplies both sheaf conditions.

proof.text: Since $I\times_TT_a=I_a$ and every $I_a\to T_a$ is finite, the finite-local-on-target theorem makes $I\to T$ finite. It is unramified directly from the stated definition. Local finite type is checked at a point in one of the open charts $I_a$, where it holds. The open subsets $I_a\times_{T_a}I_a$ cover $I\times_TI$: any point of this fibre product has a common image in some $T_a$. Above each such open the diagonal of $I/T$ is the open immersion diagonal of $I_a/T_a$. Its image is therefore open, and the inverse maps from these images to $I_a$ agree on overlaps, as inverses of the same diagonal; morphism gluing identifies the diagonal with that open subscheme. Hence the diagonal of $I/T$ is an open immersion and $I\to T$ is unramified. This explicitly supplies the locality argument without assuming flatness.

source.place: Tag 01WI (lemma-finite-local); Tag 02G4 (definition-unramified), with the open-diagonal formulation in 02GE and its elementary open-local gluing argument.

proof.text: By the 2-fibre-product convention, the base change of $\Delta_{\mathcal M/k}$ by the pair $(C,D):T\to\mathcal M\times_k\mathcal M$ has objects given by an isomorphism $C\xrightarrow{\sim}D$ after pullback. An arrow in that fibre which lies over the identity of $T$ is determined uniquely by the compatibility with the fixed $C,D$; thus this fibre groupoid is equivalent to the discrete groupoid of the just-represented isomorphism functor. The preceding construction for every $T,C,D$ therefore proves that the diagonal is represented by finite unramified schemes. For inertia specialize to $D=C$: its pullback to $T$ is $\operatorname{Aut}_T(C)=\operatorname{Isom}_T(C,C)$, so its projection is finite too. This includes the empty base and arbitrary nonreduced bases, and makes no claim that the automorphism groups themselves are trivial.

The statement is unchanged and matches the live side node; there are no new nodes. The item is not on route-pivot-dropped, has no re-split note, and cites no SGA. I checked the source, Stacks moduli-curves.tex: 0E7A (l.2568), 0E9A (l.3230), 0E9B (l.3287) and 0E9C (l.3343). Step by step: (1) J is of finite type through the chain finite-type-over-Noetherian, then open subscheme, then qc open immersion, then the affine-local closed immersion. (2) Only the smoothness clause of the coarse-projective node is used, so the stack is locally of finite type; J_B is quasi-compact and surjective on geometric points, so the stack is quasi-compact. Finite type is not inferred from the coarse space Q_g. (3) The pointed-Isom theorem needs a finite-type base, which S=J×J is; the universal curves embed in P^{r-1}_S, so its projectivity hypothesis holds; n=0 is allowed. (4) Zariski-local frames give maps to J, and finite and unramified pass to the charts by base-change permanence, which has no Noetherian hypothesis on T. Isom is not restricted to frame-preserving maps. (5)-(6) Scheme gluing has every hypothesis checked, the cocycle holds by Yoneda, no intersection is assumed affine, and local isomorphisms and their inverses glue to an isomorphism. (7) Finiteness is local on the target by clause (3); the diagonal is shown to be an open immersion by an explicit local argument. (8) The diagonal fibre is discrete by the 2-fibre-product convention, and inertia is the case D=C. Edge cases checked: empty T, characteristic dividing the automorphism order, non-Noetherian T. Recomputed closures: no node the item cites reaches the item, so there is no cycle. No existing node duplicates the item. The citer (stable abelian-level normalization) uses exactly finite type plus finite diagonal. Route: the sfb inputs are in the same unit, the pbc inputs are Mathlib leaves, and the one declared tool_use (unramified base change) is accepted. Batch-5 finding: the batch-5 closure of both targets is identical with and without the item's new edges (gain 0 nodes). Of the flagged nodes, def-trf-semistable-multipointed-pair is a general definition and lem-trf-nodal-curve-lci-criterion is a generic fact about nodal curves (nodal iff lci with unramified singular locus). Neither is a step of the trace formula or Poincare duality proofs, and neither assumption gives them, so I accept both. No fixes.

lean.statement: theorem finite_type_finite_unramified_isom (k : Type u) [Field k] (g : ℕ) (hg : 2 ≤ g) : (∃ (U : Over (Spec (.of k))) (a : BasedFunctor (discreteModuli (yoneda.obj U)) (BasedCategory.ofFunctor (forget (Spec (.of k)) g 0))), LocallyOfFiniteType U.hom ∧ QuasiCompact U.hom ∧ ∀ (T : Over (Spec (.of k))) (t : BasedFunctor (discreteModuli (yoneda.obj T)) (BasedCategory.ofFunctor (forget (Spec (.of k)) g 0))), ∃ (Z : AlgebraicSpace (Spec (.of k))) (p : Z.obj.obj ⟶ yoneda.obj T), HasSpaceBaseChange a T t Z p ∧ SpaceMapIsEtale Z T p ∧ SpaceMapIsSurjective Z T p) ∧ (∀ (T : Over (Spec (.of k))) (C D : Fiber (Spec (.of k)) g 0 T), ∃ I : Over T.left, IsFinite I.hom ∧ IsUnramified I.hom ∧ ∃ e : (Over.pullback I.hom).obj (fiberCurve C) ≅ (Over.pullback I.hom).obj (fiberCurve D), ∀ (V : Over T.left) (eV : (Over.pullback V.hom).obj (fiberCurve C) ≅ (Over.pullback V.hom).obj (fiberCurve D)), ∃! b : V ⟶ I, eV.hom.left ≫ pullback.fst (fiberCurve D).hom V.hom = MultipointedPair.parameterMap (fiberCurve C) b ≫ e.hom.left ≫ pullback.fst (fiberCurve D).hom I.hom)
lean.note: Finite type via a finite-type surjective etale atlas of the known DM stack; finite unramified diagonal via universal Isom schemes on all bases. The same-family specialization is finite inertia. fiberCurve is the canonical curve over the specified fibre base, not a chosen isomorphism class. Uses the already landed parameterMap without redefining it.
